synopsis: The booklet recommends representing simulation credibility and safety arguments in a structured form such as Goal Structuring Notation (GSN), including a GSN or Claims-Arguments-Evidence (CAE) sketch in the plan’s safety-scope section and a preliminary argument in an appendix [f8021, f14983, f12255]. GSN uses diagram shapes to frame top-level goals with context, decompose them through strategies into sub-claims, and connect them to evidence; the glossary identifies the GSN Community Standard version 3, SCSC-141C (2021), as its current definition and credits Tim Kelly with its development in the 1990s [f12249, f9705, f12251, f12250]. CAE is the main alternative, using the same three ideas with different shapes, while SACM provides a formal data model for storing and exchanging arguments [f9706, f12252, f12249]. The proposed virtual-validation claim decomposition combines GSN with NASA model-credibility practice, ASME VVUQ and integrated test-and-evaluation practice [f9725]. These recommendations are not backed by direct comparative evidence of improved heavy-machinery safety outcomes or controlled studies of readers’ understanding of assurance diagrams, neither of which the booklet found [f9722, f9888, f12257].

relations.note: Both recommend structured representation of the credibility argument, exemplified by GSN.
Both identify CAE as the main alternative to GSN.
Both report no controlled studies of readers’ understanding of GSN diagrams.
